title: Enigma message RXPSB, 1941
origin: German Army radio message Nr. 53 of 28 June 1941, enciphered on the Enigma machine and still unbroken
machine: German Army Enigma: three wheels chosen from I to V, plugboard; the keys recovered for this collection all use reflector B

form.header_meaning: Enciphered at 10:20; announced as 114 letters, the first group included; indicator ZDN QMF. With the day's settings the receiver set the wheels to ZDN and deciphered QMF to get the start position for the text.

first_group: RXPSB is not enciphered text. It told the receiver which key was in use.

transcription.by: Geoff Sullivan, Olaf Ostwald and Frode Weierud
notes: A hyphen marks a letter the receiving operator did not get. There are two.
The form holds 112 letters and marks where 114 are announced, so two more letters appear to be missing.
The copy here follows the published transcription. The facsimile was compared for layout and count, not letter by letter.

context: Radio traffic of German Army Group North during the invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa). The message was received by the radio station of the quartermaster (Ib) of the SS-Totenkopf Division.

published_hints.hint: The key of the day before, 27 June 1941: reflector B, wheels III V II, ring settings RGP, plugs AV BG CH EN FU KO MS PX RY TW. It reads the three messages of 27 June in this collection (Nr. 45, 48 and 51). It does not read RXPSB at any of the 17,576 start positions.
published_hints.checked: Run for this benchmark on 2026-11-15: the key gives the published start positions and German text for the three messages, and only gibberish for RXPSB at every start position.

published_hints.hint: The three messages of 27 June have no spaces and use X as a separator. CH is written Q. Place names are sent twice. They mention THEODOR DIV (the T Division, that is the SS-Totenkopf Division), PANZGRU VIER (Panzer Group 4), BETRIEBSSTOFF, KOLONNEN and the town ROSSIENIE. Nr. 51, sent on the same radio link as RXPSB the day before, begins MELDUNG UEBER.
published_hints.source: The three messages on https://cryptocellar.org/bgac/g-army-messages.html, read with the published key; the writing rules are also stated on https://cryptocellar.org/bgac/the-fmngi-break.html
published_hints.checked: Read for this benchmark on 2026-11-15. The decrypts contain wrong letters, so the words are given as they are meant, not as they stand letter by letter.

published_hints.hint: Those messages contain many wrong letters from reception. Two messages of this collection broken in September 2026 had 9 wrong letters in 49 and 11 in 69.
published_hints.checked: Read on the keeper's page; the wrong letters in the three messages of 27 June were seen in the decrypts.

published_hints.hint: Message MVUEH of 10 July 1941, broken in September 2026, had a key completely different from the other messages of its day, and its left-hand wheel turned over inside the message.

full_solution: The Enigma settings (wheel order, ring settings, plugboard connections and start position), the complete German plaintext, and the places where letters are missing.

verification.how: The submitted settings are entered into an Enigma simulator and must produce the submitted plaintext exactly. The answer counts once the plaintext is confirmed to be a German message. Only the standard Army Enigma with wheels I to V counts. A machine with invented wiring does not count.

notes: On 2026-11-15 Frode Weierud's site listed RXPSB as unbroken.
